lines.text: Crusaders and merchants, dukes and empires, occupation and a revolution of song. This is the story of Latvia, on the shore of the Baltic.
In the twelve hundreds, German and Danish knights came crusading to the Baltic shore, and conquered the peoples who lived there.
In 1201 they founded Riga at the mouth of the Daugava, a trading city that is today the capital.
The conquered lands became Terra Mariana, ruled by crusading orders and bishops for more than three centuries.
When it broke up, the Duchy of Courland rose in the west, small but ambitious enough to hold colonies in Tobago and the Gambia.
In 1873, Latvians gathered for their first great song festival, a tradition that would one day help set them free.
In Latvia in 1903 the painter Mark Rothko was born, later famous in America for his great glowing fields of colour.
In 1918, as empires collapsed, Latvia proclaimed its independence.
It had to fight for it. Two years of war against Soviet and German forces won the young state its freedom.
In 1940 the Soviet Union occupied Latvia, and again in 1944, beginning half a century of foreign rule.
In Riga, Mikhail Baryshnikov was born, who would become one of the great ballet dancers of the century.
Edgars Rinkevics was born, who would become president in 2023.
In the late eighties, huge crowds across the Baltic states began singing their national songs, demanding freedom without violence.
In August 1989, some two million people joined hands in a human chain across Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania. Two years later, Latvia was free.
In 2004, Latvia was among ten countries that joined the European Union, and it joined NATO the same year.
And from Latvia came Flow, Gints Zilbalodis's animated tale of a cat in a flood, which won an Oscar.
A people who sang their way to freedom now sing it at home, by the Baltic.
